source: Original paraphrase of facts reported in https://discord.com/blog/why-discord-is-switching-from-go-to-rust
article:
Discord tracks which channels and messages each user has read through a backend service called Read States. The service sits on the hot path: it is used when a user connects, when a message is sent and when a message is read, so its latency directly shapes how responsive the product feels.

The original implementation was written in Go and, despite careful tuning, showed recurring latency spikes. The team traced them to Go's memory model and garbage collector. Each Read States server keeps a least-recently-used (LRU) cache with tens of millions of entries, out of billions of Read States across the platform, to make atomic counter updates fast. When an entry is evicted it is written to the database, and every update also schedules a database write 30 seconds later.

The service did not create much garbage, but Go forces a garbage collection at least every two minutes, and each run had to scan the very large cache. That periodic scan caused the spikes.

At the same time, other teams at Discord were having good results with Rust, and the company decided to invest in frameworks and libraries for building new services fully in Rust. Porting Read States was meant both to fix the latency problem and to validate Rust as a service language. Because Rust has no garbage collector and frees memory as soon as its owner goes out of scope, an evicted Read State is released immediately instead of waiting for a collection cycle, which removes the source of the periodic pauses.

article:
On July 2, 2019, Cloudflare had a global outage that lasted 27 minutes. The trigger was a routine deployment of new rules to its Web Application Firewall (WAF) Managed Rules. One of the new rules contained a regular expression that backtracked excessively on certain inputs. Because the WAF runs on the same machines that serve HTTP and HTTPS traffic, the rule exhausted every CPU core handling that traffic across the worldwide network. Visitors to sites behind Cloudflare received 502 errors, and the company's core proxying, CDN and WAF functions went down. It was Cloudflare's first global outage in six years.

The postmortem stressed that the regular expression was only the last link in a chain. New rules were normally deployed in a simulate mode, in which they log matches without blocking traffic, but even in that mode the rules still execute, so the expensive expression consumed CPU just the same. A protection designed to stop a single rule from using excessive CPU had been removed by mistake during an earlier change. The rule update was also pushed to the entire network at once rather than gradually.

Cloudflare listed several corrective actions: re-introducing the excessive-CPU protection, adding performance profiling of every rule to the test suite, and moving away from its backtracking regex engine to engines that guarantee bounded run time, such as re2 or the Rust regex engine. The company published its detailed report ten days after the incident, and it has since been widely cited as an example of a transparent postmortem.

article:
On October 21, 2018, at 22:52 UTC, engineers replacing failing 100G optical equipment caused GitHub's primary US East Coast data center to lose connectivity with its East Coast network hub. The link came back after 43 seconds, but the brief partition set off a chain of events that degraded GitHub for 24 hours and 11 minutes.

GitHub uses Orchestrator to manage its MySQL cluster topologies and automate failover. During the partition, Orchestrator, coordinating through Raft consensus, deselected the East Coast leaders and promoted databases in the US West Coast data center, redirecting writes there. However, the East Coast primaries had already accepted a few seconds of writes that had not been replicated to the West Coast. With writes now present on both sides, the clusters could not simply fail back, and application servers in the East had to reach databases across the country, adding latency that many services were not built to tolerate.

The team chose to protect data integrity over a faster recovery. They paused webhook delivery and GitHub Pages builds, restored databases from backups and replayed writes to rebuild consistent replicas. The restore and topology stabilization took about eight hours; even after that, dozens of replicas were serving stale data, so users saw inconsistent information until the backlog cleared. GitHub reported that no user data was lost, although a few seconds of writes required manual reconciliation.

The incident showed how an automated failover system, behaving exactly as designed, can produce an outcome far worse than the original fault when cross-region topology and replication lag are not fully accounted for.

article:
On the morning of February 28, 2017, Amazon S3 in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) region became unavailable. The S3 team had been investigating why the S3 billing system was running slower than expected. At 9:37 AM PST, an authorized engineer following an established playbook ran a command meant to remove a small number of servers from one of the subsystems used by the billing process. One of the command's inputs was entered incorrectly, and a much larger set of servers was removed, including capacity supporting two subsystems that S3 needs to serve requests. Those subsystems had to be fully restarted, and while they restarted, S3 could not process requests.

The impact spread to other AWS services in the region that rely on S3, including the S3 console, new EC2 instance launches, EBS volumes that needed data from S3 snapshots, and AWS Lambda. Even the AWS Service Health Dashboard could not be updated until 11:37 AM PST, because its administration console itself depended on S3. After S3 recovered, several dependent services needed extra time to work through the backlog they had accumulated.

In response, AWS changed the tool so that it removes capacity more slowly and refuses to take a subsystem below its minimum required capacity, and it began partitioning the affected subsystems into smaller cells to limit the blast radius of future failures.

We replaced our homegrown feature flag system with a managed service. Flag evaluations now happen in the SDK from a locally cached ruleset, so they no longer add a network call to each request; median request latency fell by 8 ms. The migration covered 412 flags, of which we deleted 170 that had been fully rolled out for more than six months. The new service costs $1,900 per month, about the same as the engineering time we previously spent maintaining the old system.

Our product catalog API cached responses in Redis with a 24-hour TTL, which meant price changes could take a full day to appear. We switched to event-driven invalidation: whenever a product is updated, the catalog service publishes an event and the cache entry is deleted. Cache hit rate dropped from 97% to 94% and database load rose by roughly 10%, but stale prices disappeared from customer complaints entirely.

At Nimbus Data, we believe the future of analytics is here. Our next-generation platform empowers teams to unlock the full value of their data with unprecedented speed and simplicity. Built by engineers for engineers, it brings together the best of modern cloud architecture in a seamless, intuitive experience. Whether you are a startup or a global enterprise, our platform scales with your ambitions. Customers tell us it has transformed the way they work. We are excited to continue this journey and can't wait to share what's next. Stay tuned for more announcements in the coming months as we keep pushing the boundaries of what's possible.

Our order-processing pipeline consumes from a Kafka topic with 24 partitions. During the holiday peak, consumer lag grew to over 2 million messages and order confirmation emails arrived up to 40 minutes late. The obvious fix, adding consumers, did not help: we already had 24 consumers, one per partition, and Kafka cannot assign a partition to more than one consumer in the same group.

Profiling showed that each message triggered three sequential calls to downstream services, averaging 180 ms in total, and that consumers spent most of their time waiting on network I/O. We made two changes. First, we batched processing: consumers now pull up to 500 messages, group them by customer, and issue the downstream calls concurrently with a limit of 50 in-flight requests per consumer. Second, we increased the topic to 96 partitions to allow more parallel consumers in the future, accepting that ordering is only guaranteed within a partition, which is fine because we key messages by order ID.

Throughput per consumer rose from about 5 to about 140 messages per second. At the next peak, lag never exceeded 15,000 messages and emails went out within 30 seconds. Batching introduced a new failure mode: if one message in a batch fails, we must not commit the offsets of the whole batch as if it had succeeded. We now send failed messages to a retry topic with exponential backoff and commit the batch, which keeps the main consumers moving. Repartitioning required a brief pause in producers and a full redeploy of consumers, and next time we would plan it for a low-traffic window.

A reporting query on our 900-million-row events table had crept up to 14 seconds at p95, and dashboards were timing out. The query filtered by tenant_id and a date range, then sorted by created_at. An existing index on tenant_id alone forced Postgres to fetch every row for the tenant and sort them in memory.

We created a composite index on (tenant_id, created_at). Building it with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY avoided blocking writes, but the build took 3 hours and 20 minutes and temporarily raised replication lag on our read replicas to about 90 seconds, so we ran it on a Sunday morning. The index added 42 GB of storage.

After the change, the same query ran in 180 ms at p95. We then dropped the old single-column index, since the composite index also serves queries that filter only by tenant_id, recovering 18 GB. Write throughput on the table dropped by around 3% because each insert now maintains a larger index, which we considered acceptable.

Two lessons stood out. First, EXPLAIN ANALYZE on production-like data was essential: on our staging database, which held a fraction of the rows, the planner chose a different plan and the problem did not reproduce. Second, concurrent index builds can fail halfway and leave an invalid index behind. Ours failed on the first attempt because of a deadlock with a migration, and we had to drop the invalid index before retrying.

Event sourcing stores every change to an application's state as an immutable event instead of overwriting the current state in place. The current state of an entity is reconstructed by replaying its events in order.

The approach brings several benefits. It produces a complete audit log by design, which matters in domains like finance or healthcare, where teams must explain how data reached its current state. It makes it possible to rebuild read models from scratch, so new views of the data can be created long after the events were recorded. It also allows debugging by replaying the exact sequence of events that led to a bug.

The costs are significant and often underestimated. Event schemas become a long-term contract: once events are stored, every version must remain readable, so teams need a strategy for evolving them, such as upcasting old events when they are loaded. Replaying long histories becomes slow, which usually leads to snapshots that store the state at a point in time and add their own complexity. Queries that are trivial in a relational model, such as finding all customers in a given city, require separate read models that are updated asynchronously, which introduces eventual consistency that the product and its users must tolerate. Finally, deleting personal data to comply with privacy regulations conflicts with the idea of an immutable log and usually requires techniques such as encrypting personal fields with per-user keys that can later be destroyed.

For these reasons, event sourcing tends to work best when applied to a few core domains where the history itself has business value, rather than as the default architecture for an entire system.

When our platform team grew from four to nine engineers, on-call still worked the way it had at the beginning: whoever noticed an alert fixed it. In practice, two senior engineers handled almost every page, often at night, and one of them admitted in a retrospective that he had stopped taking vacations because he did not trust the system without him.

We started by measuring. Over three months we logged 214 pages, and 61% of them were for alerts that resolved on their own or required no action. We deleted those alerts or downgraded them to tickets, and agreed that every remaining alert had to link to a runbook describing the first steps.

Next, we introduced a weekly rotation with a primary and a secondary, so that no one was the only line of defense. New engineers shadowed two rotations before taking primary. We also started compensating on-call weeks with a day off, which leadership resisted at first but approved after we showed them the overtime numbers.

The first month was rough. Runbooks were incomplete, and two incidents escalated to the senior engineers anyway. We made it a rule that whoever handled an incident would update the runbook the next day, and by the third month escalations had dropped to roughly one per rotation.

Six months in, pages are down to about 25 per month, the load is spread across all nine engineers, and both senior engineers have taken full vacations without being contacted. The part we underestimated was cultural: people needed explicit permission to escalate and to admit they did not know a system well enough, and it took leaders modeling that behavior for it to stick.

We benchmarked our API gateway on two runtimes, Node.js 20 and Bun 1.1, to decide whether to migrate. In the summary we shared internally, we reported that Bun handled 35% more requests per second than Node.js under the same load.

The test ran on a three-node cluster, each node with 4 vCPUs and 8 GB of RAM, using a synthetic workload of 70% reads and 30% writes against a mocked backend. Node.js sustained about 18,000 requests per second before p99 latency exceeded our 200 ms threshold; Bun sustained about 22,000, an improvement of roughly 22%. Memory usage was about 15% lower with Bun.

When we repeated the test on the five-node cluster described in the setup notes, the results were similar, although one Bun node crashed twice under sustained load because of an incompatibility with a native module we use for request signing. We worked around it by replacing the module with a pure-JavaScript implementation, which reduced Bun's advantage slightly.

Our recommendation is to postpone the migration. The throughput gain is real but modest relative to the migration effort, which we estimate at six to eight engineer-weeks, and the crash suggests that our dependence on native modules is a risk we have not fully assessed. We will revisit the decision in two quarters.

I want to start with a story. Last spring, during a team offsite in a cabin outside Asheville, our CTO burned the pancakes so badly that the smoke alarm went off twice, and we spent the morning eating cereal and arguing about whether the hiking trail was 4 or 6 miles long. (It was 5.2.) It was during that hike that we first talked seriously about our Kubernetes bill.

At the time, we were spending about $48,000 per month on compute across three clusters. A colleague, who has since moved to Lisbon and now runs a small ceramics studio on the side, built a dashboard showing that average CPU utilization across our nodes was only 18%. Most services requested far more CPU and memory than they used, because engineers had copied resource settings from an old template years earlier.

We took three actions. First, we ran the Vertical Pod Autoscaler in recommendation mode for four weeks to collect real usage data, then right-sized requests for 140 deployments. Second, we moved stateless, interruption-tolerant workloads such as batch jobs and CI runners to spot instances, which now cover about 35% of our compute. Third, we consolidated the staging and QA clusters into one, using namespaces and network policies to keep them separated.

Somewhat unrelated, but our office plants also did much better after we moved them away from the air conditioning vent, which I mention only because the facilities team asked me to.

The results: monthly compute spend fell to about $29,000, a reduction of roughly 40%, and average CPU utilization rose to 52%. We had two incidents during the transition, both caused by spot instance interruptions hitting jobs that were not actually tolerant of restarts; we fixed them by adding checkpointing. The coffee at the next offsite was, thankfully, much better.

Design: Distributed rate limiting for the public API

Context. Our public API currently enforces rate limits inside each API server using an in-memory token bucket. Because traffic is spread across 30 servers behind a load balancer, a customer with a limit of 1,000 requests per minute can in practice send up to 30,000 requests per minute if their traffic is evenly distributed. Three enterprise customers exceeded their contracted limits by more than 10x in the last quarter, and one of them caused a partial outage of the search service in March.

Goals. Limits must be enforced globally across all servers with an error of no more than 5%. The rate-limit check must add less than 2 ms at p99. The system must keep serving traffic if the rate-limiting backend is unavailable. Limits must be configurable per customer and per endpoint without a deploy.

Non-goals. We are not addressing volumetric DDoS protection, which is handled at the CDN layer, and we are not changing how limits are priced or sold.

Options considered. Option A is a centralized Redis cluster storing counters, with each request performing an atomic increment. It provides accurate global limits but adds a network round trip to every request and makes Redis a critical dependency. Option B keeps local token buckets but synchronizes them every second through a gossip protocol between API servers. It adds no latency to the request path, but accuracy degrades during traffic spikes and the protocol is complex to operate. Option C is a hybrid: each server keeps a local bucket and periodically leases a portion of the customer's global quota from Redis, requesting more tokens when its local allocation runs low.

Decision. We will implement Option C. Benchmarks in a staging environment with 30 servers showed that leasing kept the enforcement error at 3.1% under steady load and 4.6% during a simulated spike, within the 5% target, while adding only 0.4 ms at p99, because most requests are served from the local bucket. Option A achieved 0.2% error but added 1.8 ms at p99 and doubled the load on Redis to about 120,000 operations per second. Option B reached 11% error during spikes.

Algorithm. Each customer has a global token bucket in Redis, refilled at the contracted rate. An API server leases tokens in batches sized at 10% of the customer's per-minute limit, with a minimum of 10 tokens. When a server's local allocation falls below 20%, it requests a new lease asynchronously, so the request path never waits for Redis. Unused tokens expire with the lease after 10 seconds, which limits how much quota a single server can hoard. The lease operation is implemented as a Lua script so that the check and the decrement are atomic.

Failure handling. If Redis is unreachable, servers fall back to local-only enforcement using the customer's limit divided by the number of healthy servers, which they learn from the service registry. Customers are never blocked because of an internal failure, but limits stay roughly in place. An alert fires if fallback mode lasts more than two minutes.

Configuration. Limits are stored in the existing configuration service and cached by API servers for 30 seconds, so changes take effect within 30 seconds without a deploy.

Responses. When a request is rejected, the API returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header and the headers X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset, so that clients can back off correctly. These headers will be documented in the public API reference.

Rollout. The new limiter will run in shadow mode for two weeks, recording what it would have rejected without blocking anything. We will compare its decisions with the expected limits per customer and contact affected customers before enforcement. Enforcement will then be enabled for 10% of customers, then 50%, then all, with a week between stages.

Risks. Customers who currently exceed their limits, knowingly or not, will start receiving 429 responses, so account managers need to be involved before enforcement. Redis becomes more important, although not critical, so we will add a replica in a second availability zone. The leasing logic is subtle, and we plan property-based tests for edge cases such as clock skew between servers and leases expiring mid-request.

Open questions. We have not decided whether internal services should go through the same system, and we need input from the billing team on whether to show rate-limit usage in the customer dashboard.

Rolling out an LLM assistant for customer support: what we learned in six months

In January we began piloting an LLM-based assistant to help our support agents answer tickets for our accounting software. The goal was not to replace agents but to draft replies that agents review, edit and send. Our support team of 45 agents handles about 18,000 tickets per month, and median first-response time had grown to 9 hours.

Phase 1: retrieval over the help center. The first version retrieved articles from our help center, about 1,200 pages, and asked the model to draft a reply grounded in them. Agents rated drafts on a 1-5 scale in the ticketing tool. In the first month the average rating was 2.6, and agents used the draft with only minor edits in 31% of tickets. Reviewing low-rated drafts showed two main problems: parts of the help center were outdated, and many tickets depended on account-specific information the model could not see, such as the customer's plan or recent invoices.

Phase 2: account context and better sources. We gave the assistant read-only tools to fetch the customer's plan, recent invoices and open tickets, and we let agents flag outdated help articles directly from the drafting interface. Over two months they flagged 140 articles, and the documentation team rewrote or archived 110 of them. The average draft rating rose to 3.7, and the share of drafts used with minor edits rose to 58%.

Phase 3: controlled experiment. To measure real impact, we ran a four-week experiment in which half of the agents, chosen at random, used the assistant and the other half did not. Agents with the assistant handled 23% more tickets per day. Median first-response time fell from 9 hours to 5.5 hours for their tickets, compared with 8.5 hours in the control group. Customer satisfaction was statistically indistinguishable between the groups, at 4.4 and 4.3 out of 5. We had expected satisfaction to improve and it did not, which suggests the gains were in speed rather than perceived quality.

Failures and safeguards. We tracked drafts that contained incorrect information. In phase 3, agents corrected factual errors in 6% of drafts, most often about tax rules that vary by region. In one case, a draft that an agent sent without careful review promised a refund the customer was not eligible for. We honored it and added a rule that any draft mentioning refunds, credits or legal terms is highlighted and requires a second review. The assistant is also limited to read-only tools: it can look up information but cannot change accounts.

Costs. Model usage costs about $0.04 per ticket, roughly $720 per month at current volume. The larger cost was engineering: two engineers spent most of the six months on integration, evaluation and feedback tooling. The documentation cleanup, which we had not planned, consumed about a third of a technical writer's time for two months.

What we would do differently. We would build the evaluation set before the first prototype; we spent the first month arguing about anecdotes instead of measuring. We would budget for content cleanup from the start, since retrieval quality was limited more by our documentation than by the model. And we underestimated agent trust: adoption only took off after we showed agents the experiment data and invited them to shape the review rules.

Next steps. Next quarter we plan to extend the assistant to the billing team's queue and to test fully automatic replies, without agent review, for a narrow set of password-reset and invoice-copy requests, which account for about 12% of tickets.

Extracting the billing domain from our monolith

Our core product has been a Ruby on Rails monolith for eight years. By last year it contained about 600,000 lines of code, the test suite took 50 minutes, and deploys were limited to twice a day because every change required a full regression run. Billing was the most painful area: it changed often because of pricing experiments, it was tightly coupled to the user and subscription models, and a billing bug in October charged 2,300 customers twice.

We decided to extract billing into a separate service using the strangler fig pattern instead of a rewrite. The idea is to route a growing share of functionality to the new service while the old code keeps running, and to remove old code only when nothing depends on it anymore.

Step 1: define the boundary. We spent three weeks mapping every place the monolith touched billing data and found 47 direct database queries against billing tables from outside the billing code, including from reporting, the admin panel and two cron jobs. Before writing any new service, we replaced those queries with calls to an internal billing module inside the monolith. That refactor alone took two months, but it gave us a single seam to redirect later.

Step 2: build the service and dual-write. The new billing service was written in Go with its own Postgres database. For six weeks the monolith wrote every billing change both to its own tables and to the new service. A nightly reconciliation job compared the two and reported differences. Early on it found about 300 mismatches per night, mostly caused by rounding differences in prorated charges and by time-zone handling at month boundaries. We fixed each class of mismatch until the job reported zero for ten consecutive nights.

Step 3: switch reads, then writes. We moved reads to the new service endpoint by endpoint, behind feature flags, starting with the invoice history page, which is read-heavy and low risk. Writes moved last, one operation at a time: plan changes first, then new subscriptions, and finally recurring charges, which we switched on the quietest billing day of the month.

Step 4: delete. Three months after the last switch, we deleted about 38,000 lines of billing code from the monolith and dropped the old tables after archiving them.

Results. The extraction took 11 months instead of the planned 6. The billing service now deploys independently several times a day, and its test suite runs in 4 minutes. There have been no double-charge incidents since the switch. The monolith's test suite went down to 41 minutes, a smaller gain than we hoped, because most of its slowness came from other areas.

What it cost. Running a second service added on-call load and another database to maintain, and cross-service calls added about 25 ms to checkout. Debugging sometimes requires following a request across two systems, which pushed us to adopt distributed tracing earlier than planned.

Would we do it again? For billing, yes: the domain changes often, has clear boundaries once the seams exist, and its failures are expensive. We are not planning to extract other domains soon; the effort was large, and for areas that change rarely, a well-structured monolith remains the better trade-off.
